To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

a single dose sitagliptin, a DPP‐4i, improves insulin secretion after meal ingestion but without increasing β cell sensitivity to glucose in healthy volunteers and in well‐controlled drug‐naïves type 2 diabetes patients, and that sitagliptin also increases active incretin hormone levels and decreases total GIP levels after meal ingestion.

a single dose DPP‐4‐inhibitor increased insulin secretion after meal ingestion, in both healthy volunteers and drug naïve, well controlled T2D patients, without increasing β‐ cell glucose sensitivity.

a single dose DPP‐4‐inhibition increases glucose‐standardized meal‐stimulated insulin secretion and incretin levels, but not β‐cell glucose‐sensitivity in healthy subjects and drug‐naive, well‐controlled subjects with type 2 diabetes
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of a DPP‐4i on β‐cell glucose‐sensitivity, incretin hormone secretion and β‐ cell function.
the effects of the incretins, glucagon‐like‐peptide‐1 (GL‐P‐1) or glucose‐dependent insulin‐otropic polypeptide on the regulation of insulin secretion in health and in type 2 diabetes.
the effects of DPP‐IV inhibitors on the incretin system.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
a single dose DPP‐4‐inhibitor sitagliptin induces a dissociated effect on different aspects of glucose‐stimulated β‐cell function after meal ingestion in T2D subjects.

a single dose DPP‐4i sitagliptin induces dissociated effects of incretin hormones, insulin secretion and β-cell sensitivity to glucose in both healthy and drug-naïve, well-controlled T2D subjects after meal ingestion.

a single dose DPP‐4 inhibiting treatment induces a dissociated effect on different aspects of the glucose‐insulin‐incretin system after meal ingestion, with increased insulin secretion and incretin levels, but without increased β‐cell glucose responsiveness.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

sitagliptin, as a single dose, improves insulin secretion in both healthy and drug‐naive T2D subjects without improving β‐cell glucose sensing, and increases active GIP and GLP‐1, but reduces their total levels.

a single dose sitagliptin increased insulin secretion and incretin levels after meal ingestion in a dose‐independent fashion, but without increasing insulin secretion in response to a given glucose concentration (β‐cell glucose sensitivity).

a single dose (100 mg sitagliptin) of DPP‐IV inhibition induced dissociated effects on β‐cell glucose‐stimulated insulin secretion and incretin hormones in healthy subjects and in drug‐naïvetype 2 diabetes patients.
The main takeaway from our work is that
DPP‐4 inhibitors have dissociated effects on incretins and β‐cell function, and this is true both in healthy volunteers and in drug‐naïvé T2D subjects with good glycemic control.
a single dose DPP‐4 inhibitory treatment increases insulin secretion, but not the glucose sensitivity of β‐cell in both healthy and drug‐naive, well‐controlled T1D subjects.
